We adapt a full-utterance speech language model using prefix supervision derived from its own complete- and partial-waveform translations, requiring neither transcripts nor human translations. We compare single-turn forced-prefix and multi-turn append-only decoding, use a confidence threshold to control the inference-time quality–latency trade-off, and vary the density of training prefixes with a separate synthesis margin. On FLEURS and CoVoST 2 in three language directions, prefix training improves quality–latency frontiers over the unadapted model, and confidence provides the broadest consistently competitive operating range. Multi-turn decoding is generally stronger at low latency; under multi-turn training, commit-calibration error falls by 63–68% overall and 68–80% at early prefixes, whereas single-turn training provides only modest overall calibration gains and no early-prefix improvement. A small synthesis margin sometimes extends the frontier to lower latency, particularly on shorter utterances, while a larger margin degrades translation quality and calibration. Prefix adaptation therefore improves simultaneous speech translation, especially under multi-turn append-only decoding, while synthesis density introduces a non-monotonic quality–latency trade-off. 1 Introduction Simultaneous speech translation begins producing a target-language rendering while the speaker is still talking. The system must therefore act on an evolving acoustic prefix, decide whether the available evidence licenses new target content, and preserve everything already shown or spoken. Waiting for the complete utterance maximizes context but incurs sentence-level latency; translating every incoming block minimizes delay but risks omissions, reordering errors, and unstable output. These decisions are especially consequential for direct speech language models. Unlike a text translation component behind streaming ASR, an end-to-end model receives no explicit word boundary or finalized transcript. Acoustic evidence arrives in time, source words may straddle blocks, and both recognition and translation uncertainty are represented inside one model. Yet modern speech language models are generally optimized for complete inputs and ordinary assistant responses, not for repeatedly extending an irrevocable translation from partial audio. Prior work addressed the analogous text problem by making a sentence-trained language model prefix-aware ( Hoang et al., 2026 ) . Its central construction uses the model’s own full-input translation as an anchor, derives targets from translations of source prefixes, and replays previously committed target text as a forced prefix. A confidence threshold then lets the model vary its lag dynamically rather than following the same read–write schedule for every sentence. Applying this principle to direct speech is not a direct modality substitution: acoustic inputs form much longer encoded sequences, arrive at model-dictated block boundaries, lack explicit lexical boundaries, and couple recognition and translation uncertainty. Efficient streaming must therefore preserve prior audio computation while representing each commit decision in a causal history of audio blocks, waits, and target emissions. Our starting point during training is a self-teacher speech language model. We ask the model to translate complete utterances and fixed-duration prefixes of the same waveform. Agreement with the full-audio translation defines how much target text can be supervised for each prefix audio. We further introduce a synthesis margin that allows the full-audio translation to rescue plausible target tokens during prefix construction, explicitly controlling the density of intermediate supervision. This training-time margin is distinct from the inference-time confidence threshold that controls when the trained model emits. The same English audio supports all target languages, and no human translation labels are required to construct the chains. Speech input also exposes a representation choice that is less consequential in the text-prefix setting. Audio inputs are much longer than text inputs, making reuse of prior computation especially important. In the single-turn forced-prefix decoding protocol, all observed audio precedes an open assistant turn containing the committed target as a forced prefix. Subsequent audio blocks are appended to the prompt. Therefore, the KV cache is retained only through the audio boundary; the full committed target must be replayed on a temporary extension before each new delta is generated, after which those target states are discarded. For long sequences, this replay can become computationally expensive, motivating the multi-turn append-only approach. In the multi-turn append-only decoding protocol, each new audio block and target delta is appended to one causal sequence, so all existing key–value states can be reused. We compare how these representations affect the quality–latency trade-off under the same training and evaluation data. At inference, a confidence threshold compares continuation and stopping evidence using only the observed audio and committed target. Sweeping this threshold gives us a quality–latency control, which we compare with fixed wait- k k and target-suffix deletion. This work makes four contributions. First, it constructs target-prefix supervision directly from partial waveforms, without transcripts or human translations. Second, it introduces a synthesis margin that controls how readily the full-audio self-translation can extend intermediate targets, providing a controlled intervention on supervision density. Third, it formulates and compares single-turn and multi-turn prompting protocols for streaming audio. Fourth, it shows that prefix adaptation improves quality–latency frontiers under both protocols and is associated with substantially better commit calibration under multi-turn decoding. 2 Related Work Simultaneous translation policies. Simultaneous translation is commonly formulated as a sequence of read and write decisions. Learned policies use reinforcement learning or supervision from oracle actions ( Gu et al., 2017 ; Zheng et al., 2020 ) , while wait- k k provides a simple fixed schedule by reading an initial source prefix and then alternating reads and writes ( Ma et al., 2019 ) . Fixed policies expose a clear latency knob but cannot adapt their delay to the uncertainty of an individual sentence. Our confidence mechanism instead lets the model decide how much target text to append after the arrival of each audio block, with a threshold controlling the required evidence for commitment. Streaming speech translation. Speech translation systems may cascade streaming ASR into text MT or translate speech directly ( Bentivogli et al., 2021 ) . Cascades benefit from mature components but expose the translation model to changing recognition hypotheses. Direct systems avoid this interface, although they must learn acoustic recognition, translation, and scheduling jointly. Streaming transducers explicitly alternate source consumption and target generation ( Cho and Esipova, 2016 ; Huang et al., 2020 ) ; retranslation systems repeatedly process the available prefix with a sentence model ( Niehues et al., 2016 ) . We retain the flexibility of prefix retranslation while constraining the target to be append-only, and we apply it directly to waveform prefixes rather than reference or ASR transcripts. Output stability and prefix supervision. Retranslation can revise earlier words, producing flicker. Prior work reduces revision through target-suffix deletion ( Arivazhagan et al., 2020 ) , forced translation ( Polák et al., 2022 ) , or agreement between consecutive hypotheses ( Liu et al., 2020 ) . Stable-prefix ideas have therefore primarily served as inference-time commit rules in retranslation systems ( Niehues et al., 2016 ; Niehues et al., 2018 ) . Self-training on partial inputs can also make a model more robust to incomplete context ( Sen et al., 2023 ) . We use agreement with the model’s unconstrained full-audio translation to create training targets and preserve the committed target at inference time, making our approach output stable by construction. Speech language models. Recent work increasingly connects speech encoders to general-purpose language models and studies their use in end-to-end speech applications ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Multi-turn speech instruction data ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , LLM-oriented simultaneous-translation frameworks ( Agostinelli et al., 2024 ) , and interleaved source–target training under latency constraints ( Fu et al., 2025 ) all move toward models that reason and generate across modalities. Our focus is narrower: adapting one offline speech language model to produce an irrevocable text translation from growing audio, while holding the full-audio self-translation fixed as the supervision anchor. Confidence and calibration. Dynamic commitment requires a score whose meaning remains useful across source positions. Neural sequence models can be miscalibrated, including in their end-of-sequence probabilities, and calibration often degrades under distribution shift ( Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) . Here, applying a model tuned for complete utterances to partial speech introduces such a train–inference mismatch, motivating direct evaluation of commit calibration. Our LLM’s native audio implementation dictates a fixed 2 2 s block cadence, so source time advances in 2 2 s waveform blocks, with a final shorter block when necessary. We call the model-visible context at boundary i i the commit-decision context : it comprises the observed audio, previously committed target, and protocol-specific causal history. This can lengthen prefix supervision at the risk of lower quality translation. 3.3 Decoding Protocols Single-turn forced-prefix decoding renders each commit-decision context as a single multimodal user prompt containing a translation instruction and the observed waveform prefix. The committed target is appended as an open assistant prefix, and the model is trained to generate only the new continuation (and the closing token). The user prompt indicates the final boundary with an end-of-audio marker. This is analogous to the successful prefix model for text-based simultaneous translation in ( Hoang et al., 2026 ) . Multi-turn append-only decoding converts cumulative commitments c 1 , … , c K c_{1},\ldots,c_{K} into append-only deltas and forms one causal record that alternates audio blocks and assistant deltas. Cross-entropy is applied to each target delta (and its closing token). The final sequence includes an end-of-audio marker before its last target delta. Both protocols are flicker-free by construction and permit the prompt and encoded audio prefix to remain cached. Multi-turn append-only decoding further reduces redundant computation by reusing previous assistant deltas. Appendix D.3 gives the complete prompt templates for both protocols. 3.4 Model and Training The base model and self-teacher are both Qwen2.5-Omni-7B ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . LoRA adapters ( Hu et al., 2022 ) are applied to the text decoder with rank 32, scale 64, and dropout 0.05 0.05 . Training begins from the same base model. Optimization uses AdamW ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) , a constant learning rate of 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} , and an effective batch size of 64. We retain checkpoints every 500 updates through a maximum of 6,000 updates. Other details of the training recipe can be found in Appendix A . Single-turn forced-prefix is trained on two equally sampled tasks, both with an empty committed target: a partial-audio example targeting prefix translation at one retained 2 2 s boundary, and a full-audio example targeting complete translations. Loss is applied only to the target text and closing token. Multi-turn append-only Each full utterance forms one causal record containing all 2 2 s audio blocks and target deltas in order. An assistant turn with no target text supervises a wait. Loss covers every assistant delta and closing token in one forward pass. 3.5 Data We train on LibriSpeech-100 and LibriSpeech-360 ( Panayotov et al., 2015 ) and Common Voice ( Ardila et al., 2020 ) , validate on a mixed set of utterances held out from the training data, and test on FLEURS ( Conneau et al., 2022 ) and CoVoST 2 ( Wang et al., 2020 ) . Appendix Table 5 summarizes the data. We reserve every 50th training utterance, using the first 400 reserved utterances for mixed validation and the remainder as a holdout. Utterance selection and 2 2 s prefix boundaries are shared across decoding protocols. Common Voice training candidates are decontaminated against CoVoST 2 by identifier, audio basename, normalized transcript, and audio hash. An analysis of the full-audio found that EN → \rightarrow ZH translations often contained conversational boilerplate, particularly in the Common Voice subset. For example, a translation of “a lot of money,” might appear as “a lot of money ; if there is any more audio content, you can continue telling me. ”.
